title: Show learner text in HTML without turning it into markup
sources: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet: HTML contexts and dangerous contexts
masterChecklist: Web-framework concepts: routing, request/response, templates, middleware, background work
Input validation, injection risks, deserialization, path traversal, secrets, dependency risk, safe subprocess use
whyItMatters: A learner's title or note may contain angle brackets or ampersands. If a page treats that text as HTML structure, the display can change in unintended ways and can become unsafe.
simpleExplanation: For ordinary text between HTML tags, escape untrusted text at the point where it is inserted into the page. Python's html.escape changes characters such as <, > and & into HTML entities, so a title like Loops displays as text rather than a bold tag. This tiny string example is not a full template engine. Different contexts—URLs, JavaScript, CSS and rich HTML—need different controls. Do not assume html.escape alone makes an arbitrary URL or script insertion safe; use a maintained framework template with automatic escaping for real pages.
mentalModel: Put a quotation in a display frame, not on the control panel that defines how the frame works.
outcomes: Escape untrusted text for a basic HTML text node.
Keep trusted markup separate from learner text.
Recognize that HTML text escaping is context-specific.
Test ordinary punctuation and markup-looking input.

realWorldExample.scenario: A study dashboard shows lesson titles entered by learners.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: A title containing markup-looking text can alter the page instead of being displayed literally.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Use a maintained template system's autoescaping for HTML text, keep markup in trusted templates, and review any URL, script or rich-HTML insertion separately.

explanation: The h1 tags are trusted page structure written by the application.
escape processes only the learner-controlled title, so its angle brackets and ampersand become displayable text entities.
The result is appropriate for this simple HTML text-node position only.
A real framework template should normally provide automatic context-aware escaping rather than hand-building pages.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Try a title containing double and single quotation marks; inspect how html.escape represents them without changing the trusted h1 tags.

procedure: Identify whether a value is trusted structure or learner-controlled data.
Choose the exact output context before choosing an encoding rule.
For plain HTML text content, escape the learner-controlled value.
Keep element names and structure fixed in trusted code or a maintained template.
Test punctuation and markup-looking titles, then review other contexts separately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Inserting learner text directly into an HTML string.
commonMistakes.why: The browser may parse parts of the text as markup.
commonMistakes.avoid: Escape data at the output boundary or use template autoescaping.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using HTML text escaping as a universal security function.
commonMistakes.why: URLs, scripts, CSS and rich HTML have different parsing rules.
commonMistakes.avoid: Apply context-specific controls and avoid dangerous dynamic contexts.

commonMistakes.why: Trusted h1 tags then display as text too.
commonMistakes.avoid: Escape only untrusted values before inserting them into trusted structure.

lab.title: Render a fictional lesson title as text
lab.safety: This is a local string-building exercise with benign markup-looking text. It does not open a browser or prove a full production template is safe.
lab.starterCode: from html import escape def title_heading(learner_title): # Require a string and escape only learner_title. # Keep h1 tags as trusted structure. pass print(title_heading('Files & paths'))
guidedSteps: Call html.escape on the title value.
Wrap only the escaped value in trusted h1 tags.
Check that <b> appears as <b> in the result.
State why the same approach is not enough for an arbitrary href or script block.
checks: The outer h1 tags remain real markup.
hints: Do not call escape on the combined h1 string.
lab.solution:
from html import escape def title_heading(learner_title): if not isinstance(learner_title, str): raise TypeError('title must be text') return '

' + escape(learner_title) + '

' result = title_heading('Files & paths') assert result == '

<b>Files</b> & paths

' print(result)
lab.solutionExplanation: Only the untrusted title is escaped. The trusted wrapper remains markup, while the title's markup-looking characters remain display text. This does not solve other HTML/URL/JS contexts.
challenges: Experiment with quotes and explain why a URL attribute needs separate validation as well as encoding.

simulation.prompt: Where should html.escape be applied in this basic heading example?
choices: To the complete finished HTML page
To the learner-controlled text before placing it between trusted tags
simulation.explanation: Escape the untrusted value for the exact output context; keep trusted template structure separate.

projectConnection.milestone: Render user-entered lesson titles as text in a trusted page template.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: Tests cover angle brackets, ampersands, quotes and non-text input; the production page uses a maintained autoescaping template and reviews non-text contexts separately.

assessment.question: What does html.escape do to < in an HTML text position?
assessment.answer: It converts it to an HTML entity such as <.
assessment.explanation: The browser displays it as text rather than starting a tag.

assessment.question: Should you escape the trusted h1 tags too?
assessment.answer: No; escape the untrusted title value before insertion.
assessment.explanation: Escaping the whole page would show the markup as text.

assessment.question: Is html.escape alone a universal solution for URLs and JavaScript?
assessment.explanation: Output encoding and validation depend on the destination context.
